They may also design or propose team structures within their own scope.

nodes.name: Politics navigation
nodes.description: Organizational politics refers to the informal dynamics of influence, interest, and power within a company. Engineering managers navigate politics by building relationships across the organization, understanding who has influence over decisions that affect their team, and advocating for their team's interests without damaging trust.

nodes.name: Cross-department collaboration
nodes.description: Cross-department collaboration involves working with teams outside of engineering, such as sales, legal, finance, or customer support, to achieve shared goals. Engineering managers represent engineering interests in these interactions and ensure that engineering constraints and timelines are understood by partners who depend on the team's output.

nodes.name: Defining and Enforcing Values
nodes.description: Team values are the principles that guide how the team works and makes decisions. Engineering managers define these values explicitly, model them in their own behavior, and hold the team accountable to them. Values only matter if they influence actual behavior, not just wall posters or onboarding slides.

nodes.name: Inclusive environment creation
nodes.description: An inclusive environment is one where people from different backgrounds, identities, and perspectives feel equally valued and able to contribute. Engineering managers create inclusion through how they run meetings, how they solicit input, how they respond to bias when it surfaces, and how they make decisions about hiring and promotion.

nodes.name: Innovation fostering
nodes.description: Innovation fostering is the practice of creating conditions where engineers feel safe to explore new ideas, experiment with different approaches, and propose changes to how the team works. Engineering managers support innovation by protecting time for exploration, celebrating learning from failure, and removing barriers to trying new things.

nodes.name: Team Traditions and Rituals
nodes.description: Team traditions and rituals are recurring activities that reinforce shared identity and culture, such as team celebrations, reading groups, or informal social time. Engineering managers invest in these practices because they build the social fabric that makes teams resilient during stressful periods.

nodes.name: Learning culture development
nodes.description: A learning culture is one where continuous development is valued and supported. Engineering managers build this by encouraging engineers to share what they learn, providing access to learning resources, discussing career growth regularly, and treating mistakes as data rather than reasons for blame.

nodes.name: Recognition programs
nodes.description: Recognition programs are structured or informal ways of acknowledging and rewarding contributions. Engineering managers give recognition frequently and specifically, making sure praise is tied to real behavior rather than generic praise. Peer recognition programs, shoutouts in team meetings, and written acknowledgment all contribute to a culture of appreciation.

nodes.name: Knowledge sharing practices
nodes.description: Knowledge sharing practices are the mechanisms through which information flows within a team and across the organization. This includes internal talks, documentation, pair programming, and wikis. Engineering managers invest in these practices because knowledge that lives only in people's heads is a risk to team resilience.

nodes.name: Social connections
nodes.description: Social connections within a team are the informal relationships that develop between colleagues. Engineering managers create opportunities for these relationships to form, especially in remote or hybrid environments, because teams with strong social bonds communicate better, collaborate more naturally, and recover from conflict more quickly.

nodes.name: Technical excellence mindset
nodes.description: A technical excellence mindset means caring deeply about the quality, reliability, and maintainability of what the team builds, not just whether it ships. Engineering managers model and reinforce this mindset by making space for refactoring, reviewing code with an eye for quality, and treating excellence as a standard rather than an aspiration.

nodes.name: Bias Recognition / Mitigation
nodes.description: Bias recognition involves identifying the cognitive patterns and structural factors that lead to unfair treatment of individuals or groups. Engineering managers actively work to recognize bias in hiring, performance evaluation, and day-to-day interactions, and put processes in place to reduce its impact on decisions.

nodes.name: Blameless Post-mortems
nodes.description: Blameless post-mortems are incident reviews conducted without assigning personal fault. The goal is to understand the systemic conditions that made the incident possible and to change those conditions. Engineering managers facilitate these sessions and model the psychological safety needed for honest discussion.

nodes.name: Emergency protocols
nodes.description: Emergency protocols define what the team does when something goes seriously wrong, such as a production outage, data breach, or major service degradation. Engineering managers ensure these protocols exist, are documented, and have been practiced before an emergency occurs, so the team can respond quickly under pressure.

nodes.name: Contingency planning
nodes.description: Contingency planning involves preparing responses to foreseeable problems before they happen. Engineering managers work with their team to identify what could go wrong in a project or system and develop plans for how to respond, including fallback options, communication templates, and escalation paths.

nodes.name: Burnout prevention
nodes.description: Burnout prevention focuses on strategies and practices aimed at minimizing and mitigating the risk of employees experiencing burnout, a state of emotional, physical, and mental exhaustion caused by prolonged or excessive stress. It involves creating a supportive work environment, promoting healthy work-life balance, and equipping individuals and teams with the tools and resources needed to manage stress effectively and maintain their well-being.

resources.title: Preventing Burnout: A Guide to Protecting Your Well-Being
Beating Burnout
How to Avoid Burnout

nodes.name: War Room Management
nodes.description: War room management refers to the practice of coordinating a focused, time-boxed response to a major incident. Engineering managers facilitate the war room by assigning clear roles, managing communication, and keeping the team focused on resolution rather than side conversations or blame.

nodes.name: Disaster recovery
nodes.description: Disaster recovery is the capability to restore systems and data after a catastrophic failure, such as data center loss or widespread data corruption. Engineering managers ensure the team has tested disaster recovery plans, understands recovery time and recovery point objectives, and can execute the plan under pressure.

nodes.name: Critical situation leadership
nodes.description: Leading a team through a critical situation involves guiding them effectively when facing unexpected challenges, high-pressure scenarios, or significant disruptions. This requires clear communication, decisive action, and a focus on maintaining team morale and productivity while navigating uncertainty and resolving the crisis at hand. It's about providing stability and direction when things are most volatile.

resources.title: How to Lead Through a Crisis
Lead how they need: adopting a situational leadership style
Situational Leadership Model Explained

nodes.name: Stakeholder Communication
nodes.description: During incidents, stakeholder communication means keeping the right people informed about what happened, what the team is doing, and when resolution is expected. Engineering managers own or coordinate this communication so engineers can stay focused on the technical problem.

nodes.name: Business continuity
nodes.description: Business continuity planning ensures that critical operations can continue during and after a disruptive event. For engineering teams, this includes planning for prolonged outages, key person dependencies, and the loss of critical systems. Engineering managers contribute to continuity plans and ensure the team is not a single point of failure.

nodes.name: Emergency staffing
nodes.description: Emergency staffing refers to the process of quickly securing and deploying personnel to address unexpected and critical situations that disrupt normal operations. This involves identifying skill gaps, finding available resources (either internal or external), and rapidly onboarding them to mitigate the impact of the emergency and restore stability. The goal is to minimize disruption and maintain essential functions during a crisis.

resources.title: Five Components of Effective Emergency Staffing Solutions

nodes.name: Service Recovery
nodes.description: Service recovery is the process of restoring a system or service to full operation after an incident. Engineering managers track the recovery plan, remove blockers, and coordinate across teams when recovery involves multiple systems or dependencies. Speed of recovery matters, but so does confidence that the fix is durable.

nodes.name: Security incident handling
nodes.description: Security incident handling covers the response to detected breaches, vulnerabilities, or unauthorized access events. Engineering managers coordinate the team's technical response, ensure security and legal teams are engaged appropriately, and manage communication with affected parties according to company policy and regulatory requirements.

nodes.name: Stress management
nodes.description: Stress management encompasses the techniques and strategies used to control and reduce the negative impacts of stress. It involves identifying stressors, understanding their effects on physical and mental well-being, and implementing coping mechanisms to maintain a healthy balance. Effective stress management aims to improve overall resilience and performance by mitigating the adverse consequences of prolonged or intense pressure.

resources.title: Stress Management
5 Steps to Rapidly Reduce Stress (Top Stress Management Techniques)

nodes.name: Post-incident analysis
nodes.description: A post-incident analysis reviews what happened during an incident to extract learnings and produce improvements. Engineering managers drive this process, ensure it happens promptly while memory is fresh, and track follow-up action items to completion. Without systematic follow-through, the same incidents tend to recur.

nodes.name: Production issues management
nodes.description: Production issues management is the ongoing practice of monitoring, triaging, and resolving problems that affect users in production. Engineering managers ensure there is a clear process for reporting and prioritizing issues, that on-call rotations are sustainable, and that recurring issues are addressed rather than just patched repeatedly.

nodes.name: Work-life balance during crises
nodes.description: Maintaining work-life balance during a crisis involves strategies and practices that help team members manage their professional responsibilities while also prioritizing their personal well-being and commitments. This includes setting boundaries, utilizing time management techniques, encouraging open communication about workload and stress, and ensuring access to resources that support mental and physical health. The goal is to prevent burnout and maintain productivity and morale during challenging times.

resources.title: The Work-Life Balance Crisis
5 Ways to Keep Your Career on Track During a Life Crisis

nodes.name: Vendor relationships
nodes.description: Vendor relationships are the ongoing partnerships with companies that provide tools, platforms, or services the engineering team depends on. Engineering managers maintain these relationships by communicating needs clearly, holding vendors accountable to SLAs, and making sure the team's dependency on any single vendor is understood and managed.

nodes.name: Customer feedback integration
nodes.description: Customer feedback integration is the practice of bringing user-reported issues, requests, and observations into the team's planning process. Engineering managers work with product and customer-facing teams to ensure feedback is structured, prioritized, and visible to engineers, so customer experience informs technical decisions.

nodes.name: Technology partnerships
nodes.description: Technology partnerships involve collaborating with external companies to build integrations, co-develop features, or share capabilities. Engineering managers evaluate the technical fit of partnerships, define integration requirements, and ensure the team has what it needs to execute without creating long-term maintenance burdens.

nodes.name: Technical customer support
nodes.description: Technical customer support involves directly helping customers resolve technical issues with the product. Engineering managers may define how engineering participates in support escalations, build tooling to help support teams self-serve, and set response time standards for issues that require engineering involvement.

nodes.name: Integration management
nodes.description: Integration management covers the work of connecting systems through APIs, webhooks, or data pipelines. Engineering managers ensure integrations are well-designed, tested, documented, and monitored, and that partner-dependent work is tracked with enough visibility to catch problems before they affect users.

nodes.name: Customer success alignment
nodes.description: Customer success alignment means ensuring the engineering team understands what customers need to achieve with the product and builds accordingly. Engineering managers bridge engineering and customer success by participating in feedback loops, attending customer calls when useful, and translating customer outcomes into technical priorities.

nodes.name: Architecture documentation
nodes.description: Architecture documentation describes how a system is structured, what components exist, how they interact, and what decisions have shaped the design. Engineering managers ensure this documentation exists, is kept current, and is accessible to new engineers joining the team. Good architecture docs reduce onboarding time and support better technical decisions.

nodes.name: API strategy
nodes.description: API strategy defines how a team designs, publishes, and evolves the APIs it offers to internal or external consumers. Engineering managers contribute to API strategy by ensuring consistency, stability, and adequate documentation, and by making decisions about versioning, deprecation, and access control.

nodes.name: Feature prioritization
nodes.description: Feature prioritization is the process of deciding which product capabilities to build and in what order. Engineering managers contribute technical perspective to prioritization by estimating effort, surfacing dependencies, and flagging when proposed features conflict with system health or strategic direction.

nodes.name: Process documentation
nodes.description: Process documentation captures how the team does its work, including development workflows, deployment procedures, and incident response steps. Engineering managers treat process documentation as a forcing function for clarifying how things actually work and reducing reliance on tribal knowledge.

nodes.name: External collaboration
nodes.description: External collaboration refers to working with engineering teams, consultants, or open source communities outside the organization. Engineering managers set expectations around contribution, communication standards, and ownership to ensure external collaboration produces value without creating dependency or security risk.

nodes.name: Technical partnerships
nodes.description: Technical partnerships are collaborations with other companies at the system level, involving shared APIs, joint infrastructure, or co-developed features. Engineering managers manage the engineering side of these partnerships, ensuring technical commitments are realistic, well-documented, and don't create architectural problems downstream.

nodes.name: Decision records
nodes.description: Decision records, often called Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), document important technical choices along with the context and trade-offs that informed them. Engineering managers encourage their use because they prevent the same decisions from being relitigated and help new team members understand why the system is built the way it is.

nodes.name: Best Practices
nodes.description: Best practices are proven approaches to common engineering challenges that the team agrees to follow. Engineering managers help establish and evolve best practices by facilitating discussions, gathering input from engineers, and ensuring practices are written down rather than assumed. Best practices should be revisited as technology and context evolve.

nodes.name: Lessons Learned
nodes.description: Lessons learned are insights captured from completed projects, incidents, or experiments that inform future work. Engineering managers create structures for capturing these learnings, such as retrospectives, post-mortems, or dedicated knowledge bases, and ensure they translate into actual changes rather than being filed and forgotten.

nodes.name: Board presentations
nodes.description: Board presentations are formal communications to a company's board of directors. Engineering managers may prepare or contribute to these when engineering investments, incidents, or strategy decisions need board-level visibility. The content must be accurate, concise, and framed in business terms rather than technical jargon.

nodes.name: Executive summaries
nodes.description: Executive summaries distill complex technical work or decisions into brief, clear communications for senior leaders. Engineering managers write these to inform decisions, request resources, or provide status on critical work. An effective executive summary leads with the conclusion and supports it with the minimum necessary detail.

nodes.name: Strategic proposals
nodes.description: Strategic proposals are documents that recommend a significant course of action, such as adopting a new technology, restructuring teams, or investing in a platform. Engineering managers write these to build consensus and secure approval, combining technical analysis with business impact framing.

nodes.name: Mentoring Programs
nodes.description: Mentoring programs are structured arrangements that pair engineers with more experienced colleagues for guidance and development. Engineering managers may run team-level mentoring or participate in company-wide programs. A good mentoring program has clear goals, regular check-ins, and a way to evaluate whether it is producing growth.

nodes.name: Budget requests
nodes.description: Budget requests are formal asks for financial resources to support engineering work. Engineering managers prepare these by quantifying the need, explaining the expected return, and anticipating questions about alternatives. A well-prepared budget request increases the likelihood of approval and demonstrates financial accountability.

nodes.name: Knowledge bases
nodes.description: A knowledge base is a searchable repository of documentation, guides, and references that the team maintains. Engineering managers champion the knowledge base as a living resource, not a static archive, by encouraging contributions, reviewing staleness, and making it a natural first stop for common questions.

nodes.name: Vision alignment
nodes.description: Vision alignment means ensuring the engineering team understands and believes in the direction the organization is heading. Engineering managers translate company vision into team-level goals, explain the connection between day-to-day work and long-term direction, and surface disconnects between stated vision and actual priorities.

nodes.name: Tech Talks
nodes.description: Tech talks are internal presentations where engineers share knowledge about a technology, project, or concept with colleagues. Engineering managers create a culture where tech talks are encouraged, scheduled regularly, and valued as part of professional development rather than treated as optional extras.

nodes.name: Migration planning
nodes.description: Migration planning covers the process of moving from one system, architecture, or technology to another. Engineering managers lead migrations by defining the target state, sequencing the work, managing dependencies, and ensuring the team has a rollback plan at each stage.

nodes.name: Brown Bags
nodes.description: Brown bag sessions are informal learning events, typically held during lunch, where someone presents or leads discussion on a topic. Engineering managers use them to facilitate knowledge sharing without requiring a formal meeting format. They work well for introducing new tools, discussing book chapters, or exploring technical ideas.

nodes.name: Legacy system retirement
nodes.description: Legacy system retirement is the process of decommissioning old software and migrating its functionality or data to newer systems. Engineering managers plan these transitions carefully, sequence dependencies correctly, and manage the risk that comes from changing systems that are still in active use by customers or other teams.

nodes.name: Change strategy
nodes.description: A change strategy is the plan for how a significant organizational or technical transition will be executed. Engineering managers develop change strategies that account for sequencing, communication, training needs, and the human side of change, recognizing that technical change often fails due to people and process factors rather than technology.

nodes.name: Technology adoption
nodes.description: Technology adoption is the process of introducing a new tool, language, framework, or platform into the team's stack. Engineering managers evaluate adoption decisions based on team learning curve, long-term maintenance, community support, and strategic fit rather than novelty. Adoption decisions should follow a deliberate trial and review process.

nodes.name: Impact assessment
nodes.description: Impact assessment is the process of evaluating how a proposed change will affect systems, teams, users, or processes before it is made. Engineering managers use impact assessments to surface unintended consequences, identify required preparation, and make better-informed decisions about whether and how to proceed with a change.

nodes.name: Tool transitions
nodes.description: Tool transitions involve switching from one tool to another, such as moving from one project management system, monitoring platform, or CI provider to another. Engineering managers plan these transitions to minimize disruption, ensure data is migrated correctly, and allow the team enough time to become proficient before the old tool is retired.

nodes.name: Reorganizations
nodes.description: Reorganizations are changes to the structure of teams, reporting lines, or organizational units. Engineering managers may initiate, lead, or be affected by reorgs. Their role is to communicate clearly about what is changing and why, protect team stability as much as possible, and help engineers adapt to new contexts.

nodes.name: Stakeholder management
nodes.description: Stakeholder management in the context of change involves identifying who is affected by a change, understanding their concerns, and communicating proactively throughout the transition. Engineering managers map stakeholders at the start of any significant change effort and tailor communication to what each group needs to know.

nodes.name: Process changes
nodes.description: Process changes are modifications to how the team plans, builds, reviews, or ships work. Engineering managers introduce process changes incrementally, communicate the reason clearly, and evaluate whether changes are producing the intended improvement. Frequent process changes without follow-through create instability rather than progress.

nodes.name: Team mergers
nodes.description: Team mergers involve combining two or more teams into one, often bringing together different cultures, codebases, or ways of working. Engineering managers leading a merger focus on establishing shared practices, integrating tooling, and building trust across the merged group before pushing for full alignment on process and culture.

nodes.name: Communication planning
nodes.description: Communication planning defines who will be told about a change, what they will be told, when, and through what channels. Engineering managers develop communication plans for significant changes to ensure the right people have accurate information at the right time, and to reduce the uncertainty that drives resistance.

nodes.name: Role transitions
nodes.description: Role transitions occur when an engineer changes function, such as moving from an individual contributor to a tech lead, or from one team to another. Engineering managers support transitions by clarifying new expectations, providing feedback during the adjustment period, and helping the engineer build credibility in their new context.

nodes.name: Resistance management
nodes.description: Resistance management involves recognizing and addressing pushback to organizational or technical changes. Engineering managers treat resistance as signal rather than obstruction, using it to uncover valid concerns, improve the change plan, or clarify misunderstandings that are driving opposition.

nodes.name: Responsibility shifts
nodes.description: Responsibility shifts happen when ownership of a system, process, or area moves from one team or person to another. Engineering managers plan these shifts carefully to ensure continuity, adequate documentation, and a clear handoff process that does not leave gaps in coverage.

nodes.name: Culture evolution
nodes.description: Culture evolution is the gradual change of a team's norms, values, and ways of working over time. Engineering managers shape culture intentionally by modeling the behaviors they want to see, adjusting practices as the team grows, and being willing to revisit and update cultural norms that no longer serve the team well.
